questions.title: Major neurotransmitter of the substantia nigra
questions.question: Which of the following acts as the major neurotransmitter in the substantia nigra?

explanations.A: Correct. The substantia nigra pars compacta contains dopaminergic neurons, so dopamine is its major neurotransmitter. These neurons form the nigrostriatal pathway that modulates movement, and their loss produces Parkinson's disease. Dopamine is the transmitter that characterises this nucleus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Noradrenaline is the transmitter of the locus coeruleus, not the substantia nigra.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acetylcholine is used by striatal interneurons and other systems, but it is not the defining transmitter of the substantia nigra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Serotonin is the transmitter of the raphe nuclei, not the substantia nigra.

questions.learning_objective: Match the substantia nigra to its dopaminergic transmitter.

questions.title: Functions of the hypothalamus
questions.question: All of the following are functions of the hypothalamus EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a function). The hypothalamus houses the body's thermostat and regulates temperature via heat-loss and heat-gain centres.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a function). It controls endocrine output through releasing/inhibiting hormones and the posterior-pituitary hormones.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a function). Hunger and satiety centres in the hypothalamus regulate food intake.
explanations.D: Correct (this is the EXCEPTION). The hypothalamus is a homeostatic and autonomic integrator, not a somatic motor centre; voluntary movement is governed by the motor cortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum. Hence control of motor function is the odd one out.

questions.learning_objective: Separate hypothalamic homeostatic roles from somatic motor control.

questions.title: Retinal cells forming the optic nerve
questions.question: Which of the following cells transmit action potentials via axons in the optic nerve?

explanations.A: Correct. Retinal ganglion cells are the output neurons of the retina: they are the only retinal cells that fire propagated action potentials, and their axons converge at the optic disc to form the optic nerve. All information leaving the eye passes through them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bipolar cells relay signals from photoreceptors with graded potentials and do not project into the optic nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amacrine cells are interneurons of the inner retina using graded signalling; they do not form optic-nerve axons.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Horizontal cells are lateral interneurons of the outer retina with graded potentials and no optic-nerve projection.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the spiking output neuron of the retina.

questions.title: Changes during near vision (accommodation)
questions.question: Which of the following occurs during near vision?

options.B: The curvature of the cornea increases
options.C: The ciliary muscles relax and decrease the tension from the suspensory ligaments
options.D: Increase in the curvature of the anterior surface of the lens

explanations.A: Incorrect. Near vision is accompanied by pupillary CONSTRICTION (part of the near reflex), so less, not more, light enters; and light entry is not the mechanism of focusing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cornea has a fixed curvature; it is the lens, not the cornea, whose curvature changes during accommodation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ciliary muscle CONTRACTS (it does not relax) during near vision; this is what slackens the zonules. The statement inverts the muscle action.
explanations.D: Correct. In accommodation the ciliary muscle contracts, relaxing the suspensory ligaments so the elastic lens bulges and the curvature of its anterior surface increases. This raises the lens's refractive power to focus near objects on the retina. The lens change is the essence of accommodation.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the lens and ciliary-muscle changes of accommodation for near vision.

questions.title: Age-related total loss of accommodation
questions.question: Total loss of accommodation in persons over 70 years of age is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cataract is an opacity of the lens causing clouded vision, not a loss of accommodation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cycloplegia is paralysis of the ciliary muscle (e.g. from drugs or nerve lesions), not the age-related process described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myopia is short-sightedness, usually from an over-long eyeball, and is unrelated to age-related loss of accommodation.
explanations.D: Correct. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation: with ageing the lens hardens and loses elasticity, so it can no longer bulge for near vision, and by about 70 years accommodation is essentially gone. This age-related total loss of accommodation is by definition presbyopia.

questions.learning_objective: Define presbyopia and distinguish it from cataract, cycloplegia and myopia.

questions.title: Rods versus cones sensitivity
questions.question: On comparison to the cones, the rods are more:

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the CONES that are concentrated in the fovea; rods are absent from the foveal centre and populate the peripheral retina.
explanations.B: Correct. Rods contain rhodopsin, are highly convergent and are far more sensitive to dim light than cones, so they mediate scotopic (night) vision. Compared with cones, rods are the dim-light detectors. This high sensitivity comes at the cost of poor acuity and no colour discrimination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Colour vision is a CONE function (three cone opsins); rods give only monochromatic vision.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fine detail (high acuity) is a cone/foveal property; rod convergence blurs detail.

questions.title: Sound transmission through the oval and round windows
questions.question: During transmission of sound waves in the cochlea:

options.A: The foot of the stapes moves inward against the oval window, and the round window bulges outward
options.B: The foot of the stapes moves inward against the round window, and the oval window bulges outward
options.C: The head of the malleus moves inward against the oval window, and the round window bulges outward
options.D: The incus moves inward against the oval window, and the round window bulges outward

explanations.A: Correct. The stapes footplate sits in the oval window; when it moves inward it displaces the incompressible cochlear fluid, and because the fluid cannot compress, the round window membrane bulges outward to accommodate the volume change. This oval-in/round-out reciprocity drives the travelling wave on the basilar membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The stapes seats on the OVAL window, not the round window; the round window is the pressure-relief membrane that bulges outward.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The malleus transmits vibration from the tympanic membrane to the incus, but it is the stapes footplate, not the malleus head, that contacts the oval window.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The incus links malleus to stapes; it does not itself seat on the oval window.

questions.learning_objective: Trace ossicular sound transmission through the oval and round windows.

questions.title: Ion that depolarizes the hair cell
questions.question: Which molecules move from the endolymph into the stereocilia and depolarize the hair cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcium entry occurs basally at the synapse to trigger transmitter release, but the apical transduction current that depolarises the hair cell is carried by potassium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chloride is not the transduction ion; the apical mechanotransduction channels admit cations, chiefly K+.
explanations.C: Correct. The endolymph bathing the stereocilia is uniquely rich in potassium; when the stereocilia bend toward the tallest row the mechanogated channels open and K+ flows from the endolymph into the hair cell, depolarising it. This unusual use of K+ influx (rather than Na+) as the depolarising current is a hallmark of hair-cell transduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sodium is the usual depolarising ion in most excitable cells, but in hair cells the endolymph is K+-rich and it is K+, not Na+, that carries the transduction current.

questions.learning_objective: Identify K+ from the endolymph as the hair-cell transduction current.

questions.title: Meaning of anosmia
questions.question: What is the meaning of anosmia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Absence of sleep is insomnia, not anosmia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Absence (loss) of taste is ageusia, a different sensory deficit.
explanations.C: Correct. Anosmia is the absence or loss of the sense of smell, caused by damage anywhere along the olfactory pathway — olfactory epithelium, nerve filaments through the cribriform plate, or the olfactory bulb/tract. Head injury with cribriform-plate fracture is a classic cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Absence of vision is blindness (amaurosis), not anosmia.

questions.learning_objective: Define anosmia and distinguish it from other sensory losses.

questions.title: Correct statement on synapse ultrastructure
questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding the synapse:

options.A: The synaptic cleft of a chemical synapse is about 20-30 um
options.B: An electrical synapse contains a tight junction permitting spread of electrical current
options.C: The axon-terminal side of the chemical synapse lacks mitochondria
options.D: The synaptic web fixes the neurotransmitter receptors to the cell membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. The chemical synaptic cleft is about 20-30 NANOmetres wide, not micrometres; the unit here is wrong by a thousand-fold.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Electrical synapses are formed by GAP junctions (connexons), not tight junctions; gap junctions allow ionic current to pass directly between cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The presynaptic axon terminal is RICH in mitochondria because transmitter packaging and release are energy-demanding; it does not lack them.
explanations.D: Correct. The postsynaptic membrane bears a filamentous, electron-dense subsynaptic (synaptic) web that anchors the neurotransmitter receptors in the membrane. Fixing receptors in register with the release site is its role, and it is the correct statement here.

questions.learning_objective: Recall synapse ultrastructure: subsynaptic web, cleft dimension, terminal mitochondria and gap-junction electrical synapses.

questions.title: Neuron type of cochlear and vestibular ganglia
questions.question: Cochlear and vestibular ganglia in the ear are examples of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Multipolar stellate neurons occur in the CNS and autonomic ganglia, not in the spiral/vestibular ganglia.
explanations.B: Correct. The cochlear (spiral) and vestibular (Scarpa's) ganglia are composed of bipolar neurons, each with a peripheral dendrite to the hair cells and a central axon in the vestibulocochlear nerve. Bipolar sensory neurons are otherwise found mainly in the retina and olfactory epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyriform (flask-shaped) multipolar neurons are the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum, not inner-ear ganglion cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Multipolar pyramidal neurons are found in the cerebral cortex, not the spiral/vestibular ganglia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the bipolar neuron type of the inner-ear sensory ganglia.

questions.title: Histology of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.question: In the retinal pigmented epithelium, the correct answer is:

options.A: Inner parts of the cells are rich in melanin pigments
options.B: It is resting on the outer limiting membrane
options.C: Their lateral cell membranes lack cellular junctions
options.D: Their microvilli interdigitate with ganglion cells

explanations.A: Correct. The inner (apical) cytoplasm and apical microvilli of the retinal pigment epithelial cells are rich in melanin granules, which absorb stray light and improve image quality. The apical processes also ensheath the photoreceptor outer segments. This apical concentration of melanin is the correct statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The RPE rests externally on Bruch's membrane, not on the outer limiting membrane (which is formed by Muller-cell junctions deeper in the neural retina).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adjacent RPE cells are joined laterally by junctional complexes (tight junctions) that form the outer blood-retinal barrier; their lateral membranes do NOT lack junctions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. RPE microvilli interdigitate with the outer segments of the rods and cones (photoreceptors), not with ganglion cells, which lie on the opposite (inner) side of the retina.

questions.learning_objective: Recall the apical-melanin and junctional histology of the retinal pigment epithelium.
